subject: Anthropology
title: Mana and Supernatural Power
description: A quick win: understand Mana and Supernatural Power.

hook.text: A chief's cloak radiates power. A warrior's spear never misses. In Polynesia, that invisible force is called mana.

buildup.text: Mana is an impersonal supernatural force believed to reside in people, objects, or places across Melanesian cultures.

discovery.text: High-status people have more mana. Sacred objects carry it. Touching a chief's possessions can be dangerous.

twist.text: Mana isn't unique to Polynesia. Similar concepts exist worldwide — qi in China, baraka in Islam, grace in Christianity.

climax.text: Mana shows that power isn't always political. In many cultures, supernatural energy underlies social authority.

punchline.text: Some power can't be seen, only felt.

quiz.question: What is mana?
options: A type of food in Polynesia
An impersonal supernatural force in people and objects

details.summary: Mana is a concept from Melanesian and Polynesian cultures describing an impersonal supernatural force that can inhabit people, objects, or places. It represents power that can be accumulated, transferred, and lost through actions and social status.
details.whyItMatters: Mana shows that supernatural power is not always tied to gods or spirits. It demonstrates how spiritual concepts can be inseparable from social hierarchy, political authority, and everyday success.
takeaways: Mana is an impersonal supernatural force in Oceanic cultures
It can be accumulated, transferred, and lost through actions
Mana connects spiritual power to social status and authority

faq.question: How does mana relate to social hierarchy?
faq.answer: In Polynesian societies, chiefs were believed to possess greater mana than commoners. Their political authority was legitimized by their spiritual power. Success in warfare, agriculture, or leadership confirmed high mana, while failure indicated its loss.

faq.question: Is mana unique to Polynesian cultures?
faq.answer: Similar concepts exist worldwide. The Iroquois have orenda, the Algonquian manitou, and the Melanesian concept differs from the Polynesian version. Impersonal supernatural force is a widespread cross-cultural idea, not unique to one region.
